title: The Persian Royal Road
summary: The Royal Road was the best-known highway of the Achaemenid Persian empire, running between Sardis in western Anatolia and Susa in Iran and credited to the reign of Darius I. Relay stations with fresh mounts let royal envoys cover the distance far faster than ordinary travellers.

uncertainty.note: Persian Heritage puts the system at about 500 BCE and says it was built or improved primarily during the 5th century BCE, crediting Darius I (r. 522-486 BCE); Encyclopaedia Iranica does not date it beyond Darius's road building. Years are astronomical (522 BCE = -521, 486 BCE = -485). Lengths differ: nearly 2,400 km (Iranica, Commerce), about 2,600 km (Iranica, Achaemenid Dynasty), 2,700 km (Persian Heritage). Stops are undated.

when.display: c. 500 BCE (reign of Darius I, 522–486 BCE)

where.modern_name: From Sardis (Sart, Turkey) through Nineveh (Mosul, Iraq) to Susa (Shush, Iran)
where.historical_name: Royal Road of the Achaemenid empire between Sardis in Asia Minor and Susa

waypoints.label: Sardis in Asia Minor, the western end of the Royal Road.
Nineveh, an Assyrian centre near which the road passed before reaching Susa, according to Persian Heritage.
Susa (modern Shush), the eastern end of the Royal Road.

importance.justification: The best-known road of the Achaemenid empire, which allowed rapid movement of trade caravans, post troops and royal inspectors across it.

sources.title: Commerce ii. In the Achaemenid period
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Iranica

beats.caption: The Royal Road links Sardis in Asia Minor, through Mesopotamia and down the Tigris, with Susa, with stations spaced along its length.
Herodotus counts 111 royal post stations on the road, with fresh mounts and remounts kept ready day and night.
Royal envoys could cover the distance from Sardis to Susa in seven days, where ordinary travel took ninety.

reviewer_note: Least sure: the date (about 500 BCE rests on Persian Heritage, a class-other site; Iranica gives none) and Nineveh as an intermediate stop, which only Persian Heritage names. Lengths differ across pages and none is stated. Wikidata points are city centres; the real road is a corridor, so uncertainty is wide.
